4:description: "Thirteen long-form beats in order, no dates, every beat mapped to a draft that already exists."
10:# Season 01, The Owned System
12:Thirteen beats, one long-form piece at a time, in this order. The season runs the frame in [World](../../DIGITAL%20TWIN/World.md): the villain is rented work and the vision is the owned system.
14:Every beat below points at a draft that already sits in `SUBSTACK/1_DRAFTS/`. No beat needs a new draft from scratch. That is deliberate, because 107 drafts is already the bottleneck.
18:A queue gives the reader no reason to open the next piece. A season names one idea, then proves it from 13 angles. Beat 1 states the argument and every later beat supplies a receipt for it.
20:The long-form pieces work like episodes. The short-form posts work like clips cut from those episodes. Each beat's Note, tweet and LinkedIn post pull one line from that beat's article, so the existing flywheel covers short-form.
22:## The beats, in order
24:The pillar codes are A for AI and Applied AI, D for DevRel and Technical Writing, and G for Growth and Content Systems. No two consecutive beats share a pillar.
26:| # | Beat | Pillar | Skill-tree node | Draft |
31:| 4 | The Content Refresh Playbook | G | Refresh an asset before writing a new one | `The Content Refresh Playbook Why 20 Minutes Beats a New Blog.md` |
44:## Beat 1 does the heavy lifting
46:`Stop Getting Good at Work That Should Not Exist` is the manifesto. It has to do four jobs in one piece, and no later beat repeats them.
53:Every later beat links back to beat 1 through `SUBSTACK/_LINK-ENGINE/magnets.tsv`. That makes the manifesto the highest-linked article in the corpus. Answer engines find it first.
57:Ten drafts tell the same story as the beat 2 flagship. A spreadsheet or a ritual became a tool you own. They will cannibalize each other in search, and they will bore any reader who opens two of them.
70:Beat 2 absorbs them. `I Built Ten Internal Apps` becomes the flagship. Each draft above becomes one named section, with its own screenshot and its own number. Ten thin posts turn into one article a reader forwards. Verify the call before you cut anything.
80:1. The season ships the beats in order. No dates, because a date you miss turns the season into a debt. Ship beat 3 before beat 4 and the order does the work a calendar would.
81:2. Every piece names its beat number and its skill-tree node in the frontmatter as `season: 01` and `beat: <n>`.
83:4. The short-form for a beat comes from that beat's article, through the existing flywheel. Never write short-form for a beat that has not shipped.
84:5. After beat 13, run the derivation again and write season 02. The villain may hold and the vocabulary counts will have changed.
92:A beat that shipped with no Note, tweet or LinkedIn post is a beat that reached nobody. That command is the only status report this season needs.

## Soundbite 1. Fill the gaps instead of acting alone

You have to support your teammates. A gap is a task the team leaves uncovered. Find where your teammates hold weak skills. Find where they push in one direction and leave a gap behind them. Then cover that gap yourself.

I learned this in Left 4 Dead. The game puts four players on one team. When each player acts alone, the instinct is to win the round alone, or to act alone even harder. Neither instinct works. The answer is to find the gaps in what your teammates already do, then fill them.

The essay version explains what support means at work. Support is not extra output. Support means you name the specific gap and you close it.

## Soundbite 2. Explaining a thing nobody has a category for

Backrooms, the 2026 A24 film, carries a line about explanation. A character struggles to explain a backroom to somebody who never saw one.

an agent that heals every failure on its own drifts toward its own guess of how your product works.

FirstRun hits that call on every red step. is this a docs bug, or does the product work this way on purpose?

@bettersayAJ wrote "self-healing is self-defeating". his fix is to ask just once.

the FirstRun design i am building this weekend:
jev, a typed judgment model, scores each failure
below 0.7, FirstRun asks me once in the terminal
my answer goes into precedents.json
the next run with the same case reads the file and skips the question

a new case costs me one question. a repeat costs me zero. #neatHack

target_audience: "Docs and DevRel engineers who run an AI agent on their own docs"

target_length: "1,800 to 2,000 words"

`jafgen --years 6` fails with `No such option: --years`. That is step 10 of the dbt DuckDB guide, run in a clean container on 10 October 2026. The guide was broken on the day it merged.

FirstRun found that break. FirstRun is the agent I built solo at neatHack, the neatlogs hackathon. It runs your quickstart in a fresh container, finds the first step that breaks, and proves the fix with a second clean run.

The docs bugs were the easy part. The harder bugs sat inside my agent, and its own reports hid them. Trusting an agent's report on itself is vibes: you use the tool and never check the output. So FirstRun runs on one rule. A fix counts as verified only when a model-free rerun in a fresh container passes.

In short:

- neatlogs raised an incident against my agent, with 25 failed-step detections at 52.8 times the baseline.
- A planner fix from neatlogs Investigate cut invented steps from 2 of 4 runs to 0 of 52.
- The verify step blocks every model call, so the agent cannot grade its own fix.
- A bisect named jafgen 0.4.6 as the release that broke the dbt guide.
- FirstRun fixed 16 docs pages and opened PRs on 3 of them. Contribution rules held back 3 more.

## FirstRun Reads, Plans, Runs, Fixes and Proves

Each run is one loop with five parts.

1. **Read.** Firecrawl pulls the docs page.
2. **Plan.** A Claude planner copies the shell commands into steps.
3. **Run.** Each step runs in a fresh `python:3.11-slim` container.
4. **Fix.** Recovery classes a failure and patches the command, with 3 attempts at most per step.
5. **Prove.** A second container reruns the patched steps with no model calls.

Each run is one neatlogs trace. A trace is the record of one run, with a span for each part of it. So when a run goes wrong, the trace shows where.

## Version 1 Passed Steps That Proved Nothing

I ran v1 on 4 quickstarts with recovery off. It finished 2. The passes taught me more than the failures did, because several passes were fake.

- A placeholder passed as a step. Chroma step 2 was `true`, a command that does nothing and exits 0.
- A fake secret passed too. `export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'` exits 0 and proves nothing.
- The planner skipped the steps that need an API key, which are the steps most likely to break.
- The plan changed between runs. The same neatlogs page gave 4 steps, then 3 steps, 5 minutes later.
- 9 of 16 steps checked only the exit code, so an error that exits 0 would pass.

Each mistake made the agent's report look better than the run was.

## neatlogs Raised an Incident Against My Own Agent

On Saturday afternoon, neatlogs raised an incident on FirstRun. It counted 25 "Execution Failed" detections against a baseline of 0.5. That is a 52.8x spike across 10 traces.

The investigation named a root cause at 66% confidence, which neatlogs labels medium. A step ran `cd my-project`, and the file check after it looked from the old folder. So the agent failed steps that worked.

[X_URL: 6acb22718680b54fcd560d61]

Commit 2de852f fixed two things. A file check now looks from the folder where the step started. Every step also runs with `set -e` now. dbt step 3 is five lines, and its failed `pip install` passed on the exit code of the last line.

MkDocs went from a false fail at 14:58 IST to verified 9 of 10 at 15:40 IST.

> **Watch out:** A last line that exits 0 says nothing about the four lines above it. Run every multi-line step with `set -e`.

## A Second Investigation Caught the Planner Inventing Steps

At 14:10 IST I made two neatlogs detections. A detection is a saved rule that flags matching spans. One of them, "planner invented a step", flagged the planner spans of 3 v1 runs.

neatlogs Investigate, in Deep mode, traced the invented steps to the planner prompt. It proposed a stricter prompt with four rules. Copy only the commands the docs write. Drop `true` placeholders. Drop fake secrets. Keep the steps that need a key.

A headless Claude Code session read the detection over the neatlogs MCP server. It applied the fix in commit 3ca6f11, with code guards and a plan cache. Real invented steps fell from 2 of 4 v1 runs to 0 of 52 runs after the fix.

## The Verify Step Blocks Every Model Call

Every other part of FirstRun depends on this step. The model that patched a step does not get to judge the patch.

`verify.py` applies the patches and starts a new container. It runs every step inside `config.block_model_calls()`, where any Claude or Jev call raises `ModelCallBlocked`. The run ends `verified` only when every runnable step passes.

A test guards the guard. `tests/test_verify.py` fails if `verify.py` imports the planner, the recovery code or the LLM module.

The Entire install shows the whole loop. Step 1 failed with `curl: command not found`, so recovery installed curl. Step 2 failed until `~/.local/bin` was on `PATH`. Then a fresh container ran all 4 steps with no model calls.

The rule has a limit, and a judge found it. A neatlogs AI judge scored 52 runs on 11 October. It agreed with the reported failed step in 46. Only 34 had every patch backed by a passing verify rerun. Runs that stopped before the clean rerun got no proof, and the judge marked them down.

## The Agent Asks a Human Once, Then Remembers

The idea came from Ajay, @bettersayAJ, who wrote "self-healing is self-defeating". An agent that heals every failure alone drifts toward its own guess about your product.

So recovery classes each failure before it patches. It checks `precedents.json` first. A precedent is a stored error signature with its class, such as docs bug or environment. A match returns the class at probability 1.0, with no model call.

A new error goes to Jev, a model that returns a typed judgement with a probability. Below 0.7 confidence, FirstRun asks the human one question. The answer goes into `precedents.json`, so the same error never asks again.

https://twitter.com/i/web/status/2108947112809378291

The dbt `No such option: --years` error is stored as a docs bug. Every later run that hits it skips the model.

## Bisect Named the Release That Broke the dbt Guide

A failed step tells you what broke, and it leaves out when. `firstrun bisect` answers the when. It binary-searches a package's releases, one fresh container per probe, with the version pinned.

On the dbt guide, `jafgen --years 6` passes on jafgen 0.3.1, released 2023-01-17. It fails on 0.4.6, released 2024-04-07. PyPI has no release between them. The guide merged on 2025-03-14, 11 months later, so it never worked in a clean environment.

The bisect took 5 probes and $0 in model calls, because it replays stored commands. The table went up as a comment on dbt PR #10149, as the next step for the maintainers.

[X_URL: 6acb227d8680b54fcd560d9a]

That PR is one of 4 that FirstRun opened on day one, each from a verified run.

- [dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149) fixes the removed `jafgen --years` flag.
- [dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10150](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10150) states the Python 3.12 floor the guide needs.
- [entireio/cli#2724](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2724) names the Linux `PATH` step after `install.sh`.
- [accuknox/help#671](https://github.com/accuknox/help/pull/671) fixes a knoxctl page that named 0.9.0 while the installer fetched 0.9.58.

https://twitter.com/i/web/status/2108903653411021062

## Version 2 Finished More Runs at a Lower Cost

The same 4 targets ran twice. v2 added the planner fix, recovery and verify.

- Quickstarts that ended passed or verified went from 2 of 4 to 3 of 4.
- Failed steps recovered went from 0 to 3.
- Fixes proven in a fresh container went from 0 to 1.
- Cost per run, from neatlogs, went from $0.0262 to $0.0200.
- Time per run went from 128 s to 201 s.

v2 runs 73 seconds longer, because a verified fix runs the whole quickstart a second time. I pay that time on purpose.

The sample is thin. Each target ran once per version, and several fixes landed within minutes of each other. So the credit for the gain is shared.

[X_URL: 6acb22772982c226ebc16ae3]

## The Business Plan Set the Agent's Spending Cap

Before the plan existed, the cap was a guess of $0.50 per run. `firstrun econ` then read 88 run traces from neatlogs. The mean run cost $0.0178, and p95 was $0.0529. The old cap sat at 30 times the mean.

cfo.ai modeled 18 months from those traces. Under the old cap, cash goes negative in month 14. At a 70% margin floor, the Scale tier cap comes out at $0.028 per run. The [public cfo.ai model](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE) holds 6 scenarios.

The executor now checks the tier cap in a `budget` span. A free-tier run on the typer quickstart stopped at step 4 with `cost budget spent: $0.0115 of $0.0108`.

[X_URL: 6aca475fe8b67041911bfd21]

> **Rule of thumb:** Measure the cost per run first. Then derive the cap from your margin floor.

## The Agent Printed a Receipt, Then Held Back 13 Pages

A docs agent earns trust in two ways. It shows the bill for every run, and it declines the work a repo's rules forbid.

**The homepage shows only real failures.** The prism on the FirstRun homepage draws errors such as `No such option: --years` and `entire: command not found`. Each one came from a real run.

[X_URL: 6acb7877727e3b9631f8a89d]

**Every run ends with a bill.** The AccuKnox knoxctl run cost $0.0453 in model use, from 10,963 input and 1,941 output tokens. Compute added $0.0020, for $0.0473 in total. That is 96.4% of the Team cap and 162.5% of the Scale cap. At Scale prices the margin is 52.5%, under the 70% floor.

The same receipt says 5 of 5 steps verified. It also carries a SHA-256 hash of each evidence file, and `firstrun receipt --check` fails when one changed. The repo holds 76 receipts.

[X_URL: 6acb787b01295dd40c110146]

**An audit costs less than one run.** Doc-audit reads a repo's git history to find stale docs pages. The first 7 audits cost $0.014609 together. dbt-core cost the most at $0.005498, for 7 Jev calls over 11,552 commits. All 7 figures are estimates from a re-run on 11 October.

[X_URL: 6acb78836222d05c0200ebdf]

**The team map found the single owner.** On the AccuKnox help docs, 9 of 9 areas rest on one person. That person is me, with 425 commits. 8 of the top 10 tasks name me, and 2 have no clear owner.

[X_URL: 6acb787f727e3b9631f8a8ac]

**The proof page lists its own gaps.** The For Judges page maps every claim to its file. It also says that 75 of 113 non-merge commits carry an Entire checkpoint trailer, and 38 do not. It says the Trail and neatlogs trace pages need a login. 360 offline tests pass on main.

[X_URL: 6acb96ac9c6f6c5901d6a763]

**The agent held back 13 pages.** FirstRun fixed and verified 16 docs pages. 3 of those pages became 4 PRs. Of the other 13, 10 needed only a container fix, so the docs were right. 3 had docs gaps.

- Flask runs `flask run` with no `--app`.
- Hypothesis gives an install line that skips pytest.
- HTTPX sets `r.encoding` after `r.text`.

The Pallets LLM policy, the Hypothesis AI policy and the HTTPX discussion-first rule ruled out an agent PR on all 3. So FirstRun opened 0 new PRs. I posted the HTTPX gap by hand as discussion #3801 on Saturday, and Polars issue #29855 the same day.

[X_URL: 6acb78736222d05c0200ebbe]

## I Would Not Build Two Cost Counters Again

FirstRun counts its own cost, and neatlogs counts it too. On 43 runs matched by start time, FirstRun's count totals $1.5253 and neatlogs totals $1.0989. FirstRun counts 39% higher, and the gap holds after the traces finalized.

The cap reads FirstRun's count, so it stops a run early and never late. That is safe, and it still gives two numbers for one fact. One counter is the next fix.

## Copy the Verify Rule Into Your Own Agent

1. Run the fix in a container that the fixing agent never touched.
2. Block every model call inside the check, and raise an error if one fires.
3. Add a test that fails if the check imports the planner or the fixer.
4. Mark a run verified only when every runnable step passes.
5. Report every other ending as not verified, and say why.

## Three Questions Get Short Answers

**Does FirstRun open a PR on its own?** No. It opens a docs PR only after the user says yes, and each PR links a public replay of its run.

**What does one run cost?** The mean is $0.0178 over 88 runs, measured by neatlogs at list price. Nothing is billed, because the runs use a subscription token.

**Can my own coding agent run it?** Yes. The site takes a docs URL and writes a prompt for your coding agent. Run `firstrun doctor --json` first as a preflight.

## Appendix

These commands come from the FirstRun README.

```bash
firstrun <url>
firstrun bisect <run> --package <pkg>
firstrun prereqs <run>
firstrun receipt RUN_ID --html
firstrun receipt --check runs/RUN_ID/receipt.json
```

- Repo: https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun
- Demo video, 2:54: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9xxgu_1bH-E

[X_URL: 6acb227d8680b54fcd560d9a]

That PR is one of 4 that FirstRun opened on day one, each from a verified run.

- [dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149) fixes the removed `jafgen --years` flag.
- [dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10150](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10150) states the Python 3.12 floor the guide needs.
- [entireio/cli#2724](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2724) names the Linux `PATH` step after `install.sh`.
- [accuknox/help#671](https://github.com/accuknox/help/pull/671) fixes a knoxctl page that named 0.9.0 while the installer fetched 0.9.58.

https://twitter.com/i/web/status/2108903653411021062

## Version 2 Finished More Runs at a Lower Cost

The same 4 targets ran twice. v2 added the planner fix, recovery and verify.

- Quickstarts that ended passed or verified went from 2 of 4 to 3 of 4.
- Failed steps recovered went from 0 to 3.
- Fixes proven in a fresh container went from 0 to 1.
- Cost per run, from neatlogs, went from $0.0262 to $0.0200.
- Time per run went from 128 s to 201 s.

v2 runs 73 seconds longer, because a verified fix runs the whole quickstart a second time. I pay that time on purpose.

The sample is thin. Each target ran once per version, and several fixes landed within minutes of each other. So the credit for the gain is shared.

[X_URL: 6acb22772982c226ebc16ae3]

## The Business Plan Set the Agent's Spending Cap

Before the plan existed, the cap was a guess of $0.50 per run. `firstrun econ` then read 88 run traces from neatlogs. The mean run cost $0.0178, and p95 was $0.0529. The old cap sat at 30 times the mean.

cfo.ai modeled 18 months from those traces. Under the old cap, cash goes negative in month 14. At a 70% margin floor, the Scale tier cap comes out at $0.028 per run. The [public cfo.ai model](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE) holds 6 scenarios.

The executor now checks the tier cap in a `budget` span. A free-tier run on the typer quickstart stopped at step 4 with `cost budget spent: $0.0115 of $0.0108`.

[X_URL: 6aca475fe8b67041911bfd21]

> **Rule of thumb:** Measure the cost per run first. Then derive the cap from your margin floor.

## The Agent Printed a Receipt, Then Held Back 13 Pages

A docs agent earns trust in two ways. It shows the bill for every run, and it declines the work a repo's rules forbid.

**The homepage shows only real failures.** The prism on the FirstRun homepage draws errors such as `No such option: --years` and `entire: command not found`. Each one came from a real run.

[X_URL: 6acb7877727e3b9631f8a89d]

**Every run ends with a bill.** The AccuKnox knoxctl run cost $0.0453 in model use, from 10,963 input and 1,941 output tokens. Compute added $0.0020, for $0.0473 in total. That is 96.4% of the Team cap and 162.5% of the Scale cap. At Scale prices the margin is 52.5%, under the 70% floor.

The same receipt says 5 of 5 steps verified. It also carries a SHA-256 hash of each evidence file, and `firstrun receipt --check` fails when one changed. The repo holds 76 receipts.

[X_URL: 6acb787b01295dd40c110146]

**An audit costs less than one run.** Doc-audit reads a repo's git history to find stale docs pages. The first 7 audits cost $0.014609 together. dbt-core cost the most at $0.005498, for 7 Jev calls over 11,552 commits. All 7 figures are estimates from a re-run on 11 October.

[X_URL: 6acb78836222d05c0200ebdf]

**The team map found the single owner.** On the AccuKnox help docs, 9 of 9 areas rest on one person. That person is me, with 425 commits. 8 of the top 10 tasks name me, and 2 have no clear owner.

[X_URL: 6acb787f727e3b9631f8a8ac]

**The proof page lists its own gaps.** The For Judges page maps every claim to its file. It also says that 75 of 113 non-merge commits carry an Entire checkpoint trailer, and 38 do not. It says the Trail and neatlogs trace pages need a login. 360 offline tests pass on main.

[X_URL: 6acb96ac9c6f6c5901d6a763]

**The agent held back 13 pages.** FirstRun fixed and verified 16 docs pages. 3 of those pages became 4 PRs. Of the other 13, 10 needed only a container fix, so the docs were right. 3 had docs gaps.

- Flask runs `flask run` with no `--app`.
- Hypothesis gives an install line that skips pytest.
- HTTPX sets `r.encoding` after `r.text`.

The Pallets LLM policy, the Hypothesis AI policy and the HTTPX discussion-first rule ruled out an agent PR on all 3. So FirstRun opened 0 new PRs. I posted the HTTPX gap by hand as discussion #3801 on Saturday, and Polars issue #29855 the same day.

[X_URL: 6acb78736222d05c0200ebbe]

## I Would Not Build Two Cost Counters Again

FirstRun counts its own cost, and neatlogs counts it too. On 43 runs matched by start time, FirstRun's count totals $1.5253 and neatlogs totals $1.0989. FirstRun counts 39% higher, and the gap holds after the traces finalized.

The cap reads FirstRun's count, so it stops a run early and never late. That is safe, and it still gives two numbers for one fact. One counter is the next fix.

## Copy the Verify Rule Into Your Own Agent

1. Run the fix in a container that the fixing agent never touched.
2. Block every model call inside the check, and raise an error if one fires.
3. Add a test that fails if the check imports the planner or the fixer.
4. Mark a run verified only when every runnable step passes.
5. Report every other ending as not verified, and say why.

## Three Questions Get Short Answers

**Does FirstRun open a PR on its own?** No. It opens a docs PR only after the user says yes, and each PR links a public replay of its run.

**What does one run cost?** The mean is $0.0178 over 88 runs, measured by neatlogs at list price. Nothing is billed, because the runs use a subscription token.

**Can my own coding agent run it?** Yes. The site takes a docs URL and writes a prompt for your coding agent. Run `firstrun doctor --json` first as a preflight.

## Appendix

These commands come from the FirstRun README.

```bash
firstrun <url>
firstrun bisect <run> --package <pkg>
firstrun prereqs <run>
firstrun receipt RUN_ID --html
firstrun receipt --check runs/RUN_ID/receipt.json
```

- Demo video, 2:54: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9xxgu_1bH-E

content.content:
19	
20	`jafgen --years 6` fails with `No such option: --years`. That is step 10 of the dbt DuckDB guide, run in a clean container on 10 October 2026. The guide was broken on the day it merged.
21	
22	FirstRun found that break. FirstRun is the agent I built solo at neatHack, the neatlogs hackathon, to test agent quickstarts and docs. It runs a quickstart in a fresh container, finds the first broken step, and proves the fix with a second clean run.
23	
24	The docs bugs were the easy part. The harder bugs sat inside my agent, and its own reports hid them. Trusting an agent's report on itself is vibes: you use the tool and never check the output. So FirstRun runs on one rule. A fix counts as verified only when a model-free rerun in a fresh container passes.
25	
26	In short:
27	
28	- neatlogs raised an incident against my agent, at 52.8 times the baseline.
29	- A planner fix from neatlogs Investigate cut invented steps from 2 of 4 runs to 0 of 52.
30	- The verify step blocks every model call, so the agent cannot grade its own fix.
31	- A bisect named jafgen 0.4.6 as the release that broke the dbt guide.
32	- FirstRun fixed 16 docs pages, and contribution rules held back 3 PRs.
33	
34	## FirstRun Reads, Plans, Runs, Fixes and Proves
35	
36	Each run is one loop with five parts.
37	
38	1. **Read.** Firecrawl pulls the docs page.
39	2. **Plan.** A Claude planner copies the shell commands into steps.
40	3. **Run.** Each step runs in a fresh `python:3.11-slim` container.
41	4. **Fix.** Recovery classes a failure and patches the command, with 3 attempts at most per step.
42	5. **Prove.** A second container reruns the patched steps with no model calls.
43	
44	Each run is one neatlogs trace, with a span for each part, so a bad run shows where it went wrong.
45	
46	## Version 1 Passed Steps That Proved Nothing
47	
48	I ran v1 on 4 quickstarts with recovery off. The passes taught me more than the failures, because several passes were fake.
49	
50	- A placeholder passed as a step. Chroma step 2 was `true`, a command that does nothing and exits 0.
51	- A fake secret passed too. `export OPENAI_API_KEY='sk-...'` exits 0 and proves nothing.
52	- The planner skipped the steps that need an API key, which are the steps most likely to break.
53	- The plan changed between runs. The same neatlogs page gave 4 steps, then 3 steps, 5 minutes later.
54	- 9 of 16 steps checked only the exit code, so an error that exits 0 would pass.
55	
56	Each mistake made the agent's report look better than the run was.
57	
58	## An Incident Report Named My Agent as the Cause
59	
60	On Saturday afternoon, neatlogs raised an incident on FirstRun. It counted 25 "Execution Failed" detections against a baseline of 0.5. That is a 52.8x spike across 10 traces.
61	
62	The investigation named a root cause at 66% confidence, which neatlogs labels medium. A step ran `cd my-project`, and the file check after it looked from the old folder. So the agent failed steps that worked.
63	
64	[X_URL: 6acb22718680b54fcd560d61]
65	
66	Commit 2de852f fixed two things. A file check now looks from the folder where the step started. Every step also runs with `set -e` now. dbt step 3 is five lines, and its failed `pip install` passed on the exit code of the last line.
67	
68	MkDocs went from a false fail at 14:58 IST to verified 9 of 10 at 15:40 IST.
69	
70	> **Watch out:** A last line that exits 0 says nothing about the four lines above it. Run every multi-line step with `set -e`.
71	
72	## A Second Investigation Caught the Planner Inventing Steps
73	
74	At 14:10 IST I made two neatlogs detections. A detection is a saved rule that flags matching spans. One of them, "planner invented a step", flagged the planner spans of 3 v1 runs.
75	
76	neatlogs Investigate traced the invented steps to the planner prompt. It proposed a stricter prompt that copies only the commands the docs write.
77	
78	A headless Claude Code session read the detection over the neatlogs MCP server, the interface an agent uses to query neatlogs. It applied the fix in commit 3ca6f11. Real invented steps fell from 2 of 4 v1 runs to 0 of 52 runs after the fix.
79	
80	## The Verify Step Blocks Every Model Call
81	
82	The model that patched a step does not get to judge the patch.
83	
84	`verify.py` applies the patches and starts a new container. It runs every step inside `config.block_model_calls()`, where any Claude or Jev call raises `ModelCallBlocked`. The run ends `verified` only when every runnable step passes.
85	
86	A test guards the guard. `tests/test_verify.py` fails if `verify.py` imports the planner, the recovery code or the LLM module.
87	
88	On the Entire install, recovery added curl and a `PATH` line. Then a fresh container ran all 4 steps with no model calls.
89	
90	The rule has a limit. A neatlogs AI judge scored 52 runs on 11 October. It agreed with the reported failed step in 46. Only 34 had every patch backed by a passing verify rerun. Runs that stopped before the clean rerun got no proof, and the judge marked them down.
91	
92	## The Agent Asks a Human Once, Then Remembers
93	
94	The idea came from Ajay, @bettersayAJ, who wrote "self-healing is self-defeating". So recovery classes each failure before it patches. It checks `precedents.json` first. A precedent is a stored error signature with its class, such as docs bug or environment. A match returns the class at probability 1.0, with no model call.
95	
96	A new error goes to Jev, a model that returns a typed judgement with a probability. Below 0.7 confidence, FirstRun asks the human one question. The answer goes into `precedents.json`, so the same error never asks again.
97	
98	https://twitter.com/i/web/status/2108947112809378291
99	
100	## Bisect Named the Release That Broke the DuckDB Guide
101	
102	`firstrun bisect` finds when a step broke. It binary-searches a package's releases, one fresh container per probe, with the version pinned.
103	
104	On the dbt guide, `jafgen --years 6` passes on jafgen 0.3.1, released 2023-01-17. It fails on 0.4.6, released 2024-04-07. PyPI has no release between them. The guide merged on 2025-03-14, 11 months later, so it never worked in a clean environment.
105	
106	The bisect took 5 probes and $0 in model calls, because it replays stored commands. The table went up as a comment on dbt PR #10149.
107	
108	[X_URL: 6acb227d8680b54fcd560d9a]
109	
110	FirstRun opened 4 PRs on day one, each from a verified run.
111	
112	- [dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10149](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10149) fixes the removed `jafgen --years` flag.
113	- [dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10150](https://github.com/dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com/pull/10150) states the Python 3.12 floor the guide needs.
114	- [entireio/cli#2724](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2724) names the Linux `PATH` step after `install.sh`.
115	- [accuknox/help#671](https://github.com/accuknox/help/pull/671) fixes a knoxctl page that named 0.9.0 while the installer fetched 0.9.58.
116	
117	https://twitter.com/i/web/status/2108903653411021062
118	
119	## Version 2 Finished More Runs at a Lower Cost
120	
121	The same 4 targets ran twice. v2 added the planner fix, recovery and verify.
122	
123	- Quickstarts that ended passed or verified went from 2 of 4 to 3 of 4.
124	- Failed steps recovered went from 0 to 3.
125	- Fixes proven in a fresh container went from 0 to 1.
126	- Cost per run, from neatlogs, went from $0.0262 to $0.0200.
127	- Time per run went from 128 s to 201 s.
128	
129	v2 runs 73 seconds longer, because a verified fix runs the whole quickstart twice.
130	
131	The sample is thin. Each target ran once per version, and several fixes landed together, so they share the credit.
132	
133	[X_URL: 6acb22772982c226ebc16ae3]
134	
135	## The Business Plan Set the Agent's Spending Cap
136	
137	Before the plan existed, the cap was a guess of $0.50 per run. Then `firstrun econ` read 88 run traces from neatlogs. The old cap sat at 30 times the mean run cost of $0.0178.
138	
139	cfo.ai modeled 18 months from those traces. Under the old cap, cash goes negative in month 14. At a 70% margin floor, the Scale tier cap comes out at $0.028 per run. The [cfo.ai model](https://cfo.ai/s/_u5lbrHIl9KX_JQE) is public.
140	
141	The executor now checks the tier cap in a `budget` span. A free-tier run on the typer quickstart stopped at step 4 with `cost budget spent: $0.0115 of $0.0108`.
142	
143	[X_URL: 6aca475fe8b67041911bfd21]
144	
145	> **Rule of thumb:** Measure the cost per run first. Then derive the cap from your margin floor.
146	
147	## The Agent Printed a Receipt, Then Held Back 13 Pages
148	
149	A docs agent earns trust when it shows the bill for every run and declines work a repo's rules forbid.
150	
151	**The homepage shows only real failures.** Each error on the FirstRun homepage, such as `entire: command not found`, came from a real run.
152	
153	[X_URL: 6acb7877727e3b9631f8a89d]
154	
155	**Every run ends with a bill.** The AccuKnox knoxctl run cost $0.0453 in model use, from 10,963 input and 1,941 output tokens. Compute added $0.0020, for $0.0473 in total. That is 96.4% of the Team cap and 162.5% of the Scale cap. At Scale prices the margin is 52.5%, under the 70% floor.
156	
157	The receipt also hashes each evidence file, and `firstrun receipt --check` fails when one changed.
158	
159	[X_URL: 6acb787b01295dd40c110146]
160	
161	**An audit costs less than one run.** Doc-audit reads a repo's git history to find stale docs pages. The first 7 audits cost $0.014609 together. dbt-core cost the most at $0.005498, for 7 Jev calls over 11,552 commits. All 7 figures are estimates from a re-run on 11 October.
162	
163	[X_URL: 6acb78836222d05c0200ebdf]
164	
165	**The team map found the single owner.** On the AccuKnox help docs, 9 of 9 areas rest on one person. That person is me, with 425 commits. 8 of the top 10 tasks name me, and 2 have no clear owner.
166	
167	[X_URL: 6acb787f727e3b9631f8a8ac]
168	
169	**The proof page lists its own gaps.** The For Judges page maps every claim to its file. It also says that 38 of 113 non-merge commits carry no Entire checkpoint, and that two proof pages need a login.
170	
171	[X_URL: 6acb96ac9c6f6c5901d6a763]
172	
173	**The agent held back 13 pages.** FirstRun fixed and verified 16 docs pages. 3 of those pages became 4 PRs. Of the other 13, 10 needed only a container fix, so the docs were right. 3 had docs gaps.
174	
175	- Flask runs `flask run` with no `--app`.
176	- Hypothesis gives an install line that skips pytest.
177	- HTTPX sets `r.encoding` after `r.text`.
178	
179	The Pallets LLM policy, the Hypothesis AI policy and the HTTPX discussion-first rule ruled out an agent PR on all 3. So FirstRun opened 0 new PRs. I posted the HTTPX gap by hand as discussion #3801 on Saturday, and Polars issue #29855 the same day.
180	
181	[X_URL: 6acb78736222d05c0200ebbe]
182	
183	## I Would Not Build Two Cost Counters Again
184	
185	FirstRun and neatlogs each count the cost of a run. On 43 matched runs, FirstRun counts 39% higher. The cap reads FirstRun's count, so it stops a run early and never late. That is safe, and it still gives two numbers for one fact. I will merge them into one counter next.
186	
187	## Copy the Verify Rule Into Your Own Agent
188	
189	1. Run the fix in a container that the fixing agent never touched.
190	2. Block every model call inside the check, and raise an error if one fires.
191	3. Add a test that fails if the check imports the planner or the fixer.
192	4. Mark a run verified only when every runnable step passes.
193	5. Report every other ending as not verified, and say why.
194	
195	## Three Questions Get Short Answers
196	
197	**Does FirstRun open a PR on its own?** No. It opens a docs PR only after the user says yes.
198	
199	**What does one run cost?** The mean is $0.0178 over 88 runs, at list price.
200	
201	**Can my own coding agent run it?** Yes. The site takes a docs URL and writes a prompt for your coding agent.
202	
203	## Appendix
204	
205	```bash
206	firstrun <url>
207	firstrun bisect <run> --package <pkg>
208	firstrun prereqs <run>
209	firstrun receipt RUN_ID --html
210	firstrun receipt --check runs/RUN_ID/receipt.json
211	```
212	
213	- Site: https://firstrun.atharvashah.com
214	- Repo: https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun
215	- Demo video, 2:54: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9xxgu_1bH-E
